name: When the Banks Stepped Back
deck: Post-2008 Basel III capital requirements and post-2022 regional bank failures forced regulated lenders to shrink credit supply and raise capital ratios, creating a regulatory vacuum that alternative asset managers rushed to fill with private credit, asset-based finance, and direct lending.
core_bet: The structural inflection that enabled private-capital colonization was regulatory asymmetry: banks were constrained by Basel III (2010-2020 rollout), credit-risk weighting (continuously tightened 2010-2022), and deposit-base pressure (accelerated 2022-2023 after regional bank failures), while non-bank alternatives faced comparatively loose oversight. This asymmetry is now permanent. Regulated banks like PNC are retreating to high-margin relationship lending and capital-light fee income. Private-credit platforms like Apollo, KKR, and Ares have filled the gap with $1T+ of deployed capital in illiquid, higher-yielding strategies that banks can no longer or will not underwrite.

numbers.label: KKR ANI conversion rate (capital deployed vs AUM)

mechanism: Basel III tightened regulatory capital requirements for banks in two distinct phases: first during 2010-2020, requiring higher Tier 1 capital ratios and more conservative risk-weighting of assets; and second during 2023-2025 (after regional bank failures), when regulators further tightened oversight and banks voluntarily raised capital ratios to avoid regulatory scrutiny. This made certain lending products economically unviable for banks: illiquid loans to mid-market companies, small-business lending, real-estate development loans, and structured credit. The cost-of-capital math changed materially. A regional bank like PNC in 2025 had to choose between holding significantly more capital against risky loans or exiting the business entirely. The regulatory leverage made capital-intensive lending economically irrational. Many banks chose to exit.

Regional bank failures in 2023-2024 (SVB in March 2023, Signature in March 2023, First Republic in May 2023) created an acceleration shock in regulatory tightening. These banks had deployed capital into longer-duration assets and faced deposit-flight risk when the Fed raised rates in 2022-2023. Regulators tightened oversight even further after the collapses, and surviving banks like PNC faced two choices: raise capital ratios to hedge against deposit-flight risk, or shrink the balance sheet. Most chose to raise capital ratios, which meant reducing leverage and therefore reducing balance-sheet lending capacity. The banks' withdrawal created a credit supply shock: trillions of dollars in credit demand that had historically been served by banks now had no obvious regulated supply source.

Alternative asset managers stepped into the gap systematically during 2023-2025. Private-credit platforms like Apollo, KKR, and Ares built or expanded dedicated origination teams, balance-sheet capacity (especially through insurance subsidiaries like Athene and Global Atlantic), and fee structures designed to monetize less-liquid, higher-yielding credit. Apollo's 2025 origination of $300B+ shows the scale of credit creation that moved out of banks. KKR's integration of insurance economics through Global Atlantic (a $330B AUM insurance company) allows the firm to deploy capital at longer durations and lower expected returns than pure PE, effectively competing in the middle-market credit space that banks were abandoning. Ares' $156B of available capital (dry powder + undeployed) sits ready to execute and continues to raise capital (raised $129B in capital in 2025). This is not opportunistic gap-filling; it is systematic capital reallocation.

The regulatory asymmetry is the structural permanence. Non-bank lenders face less stringent capital requirements, less-strict loan-documentation rules, and greater flexibility in pricing and structure. They can hold illiquid assets longer without mark-to-market pressure (funds are not daily-redeemable). They can take credit-quality risk that banks cannot (no FDIC insurance requirement, no regulatory pressure on loan-loss reserves). They can price at 3-5% management fees plus carry on returns—significantly higher than traditional bank lending (typically 50-150 bps). The result is a permanent economic arbitrage: alternative platforms can monetize credit creation that banks no longer can or will undertake, because the regulatory and capital cost of doing so is prohibitively high for regulated lenders. This arbitrage did not exist before 2010; by 2025, it was structural and permanent.
why_now: Basel III was written in 2010, implemented gradually through 2015-2020, and tightened further after 2023. Fifteen years of regulatory pressure (2010-2025) has structurally reset the economics of bank lending. The turning points were: 2013-2015 (when large banks completed Basel III implementation and reduced leverage); 2020-2022 (when COVID relief inflated bank balance sheets temporarily, but regulatory pressure remained); 2023-2025 (when regional bank failures forced tightening and surviving banks raised capital ratios). At the same time, private markets have grown and institutionalized in parallel. Insurance companies and pension funds now have appetite for private credit that they did not have in 2008—Athene has $330B of AUM, much of it dedicated to credit strategies. Technology has improved for underwriting and servicing less-liquid credit (data analytics, modeling, syndication platforms). Fee structures have matured. The timing is now: there is enough supply of capital (insurance float, institutional AUM, family offices, endowments) and enough demand for credit (the lending gap from retreating banks) that alternatives have permanent scale. The regulatory difference is also more durable now because political and regulatory will to re-regulate non-banks is weak—they are not seen as systemically critical yet. Banks, by contrast, face permanent regulatory pressure. This is a structural 15-year shift (2010-2025), not a cycle. It is now because the accumulation of regulatory pressure, capital-market growth, and institutional-investor appetite has reached critical mass.
who_pays: Small-to-mid-market companies and borrowers pay the cost through higher lending rates, tighter covenants, and higher required equity contributions. Private-credit platforms charge 3-5% management fees plus carry on returns—significantly higher than traditional bank lending (typically 50-150 bps on yields). Borrowers also face less flexibility: bank loans have standard documentation; private credit has custom terms that often favor the lender. Retail savers and pension-fund beneficiaries pay indirectly: the capital flowing into private credit is capital not flowing into public-market infrastructure (regulated utilities, transportation) or bank deposits, which shifts yields and risk allocation. Workers and communities in regions where small-business lending has dried up lose access to affordable credit for local business expansion. Regional banks that survived 2023 but cannot compete with private capital on returns lose market share and deposit base.
who_profits: Alternative asset managers capture fee and carry spread on trillions of dollars of private credit. Apollo's 2025 fee-related earnings of about $2.5B plus spread-related earnings of about $3.4B (Athene insurance operations) is the proof of permanent profit extraction. KKR's full-year 2025 FRE of about $3.7B, TOE of about $5.0B, ANI of about $4.4B shows the integrated model (insurance + credit + PE) is generating permanent earnings. Ares' 2025 AUM of $622.5B with 25% management-fee growth YoY and fee-related earnings of about $1.78B shows the model is scaling. Institutional LPs (pensions, endowments, insurance companies, family offices) benefit from higher-yielding strategies in private credit, though at increased liquidity and credit risk. Large corporations with scale can still access bank credit at reasonable rates; middle-market and smaller firms are funneled into private credit where pricing is 100-200bps higher. The entire gains distribution is tilted toward alternative managers.
tension: The first tension is that non-bank credit is less stable and more pro-cyclical than bank credit. Banks have FDIC insurance and central-bank backstops; they can hold illiquid assets through downturns. Non-bank lenders have investor capital and reputation; they face redemption pressure and mark-to-market in downturns. In a credit crisis, private-credit platforms must either redeem LPs at losses or gate redemptions, creating sell pressure and contagion. The second tension is that this model depends on favorable credit conditions and low defaults. Apollo's spread earnings depend on Athene's portfolio performing well and credit defaults staying low. If credit conditions tighten (2026 risk if rates stay high), origination slows, refinancing pressure builds, defaults accelerate, and the model compresses. A third tension is political risk. If private credit is seen as destabilizing or unfair (high fees, capital extraction), regulation could tighten suddenly, shrinking available capital and repricing the entire system. A final tension is that the regulatory asymmetry is not sustainable long-term. If non-banks grow large enough to pose systemic risk (Apollo is $938B AUM, KKR is $744B, Ares is $622.5B), regulation will eventually follow. That could force capital minimums, fee caps, or leverage restrictions on private platforms, shrinking returns and available capital.
surprising_part: What stands out is how thoroughly banks have ceded the middle market between 2010 and 2025. PNC is still a massive franchise ($7.0B annual net income in 2025), but it is focused on the top 1,000 companies and ultra-high-net-worth individuals. Middle-market lending has moved almost entirely into private platforms by 2025. The speed of this transition—essentially 2018-2025—is remarkable. A second surprise is how effectively alternative platforms have integrated insurance and balance-sheet economics to solve the duration and leverage constraints that fund-based models face. Apollo's Athene insurance strategy is not a side business; it is the core earnings engine generating $3.4B of spread-related earnings. KKR's Global Atlantic acquisition ($330B AUM) is central to monetization at scale. Ares' capital raises stayed strong in 2025 despite regulatory scrutiny. This is not opportunistic; it is deliberate structural engineering. A third surprise is the lack of regulatory response. Banks faced tightening for 15 years; private platforms have grown unfettered. By 2025, alternative managers controlled $1T+ of deployed capital in illiquid credit, yet faced minimal regulatory scrutiny. That asymmetry is the core of the model.
one_sentence: Regulatory constraints on banks (Basel III 2010-2025, regional failures 2023-2025) created a permanent capital supply gap that private alternatives filled with higher fees, looser structures, and insurance-backed balance sheets.
societal_stake: The migration of credit creation from banks to private alternatives is a fundamental shift in access and cost. Banks are utility-like intermediaries with public accountability, deposit insurance, and central-bank backstops. Private-credit platforms are profit-maximizing entities with limited public obligation and no backstops. This means: (1) smaller companies and entrepreneurs pay 100-200bps more to borrow; (2) credit becomes less stable and more cyclical (no FDIC insurance, no Federal Reserve backstop); (3) fee capture is higher (3-5% management fees vs 50-150 bps in bank lending), reducing real-economy deployment of capital; (4) the system is more fragile because non-bank lenders have no public backstop and face redemption pressure in downturns. If this pattern continues through 2026-2030, middle-market credit will remain permanently expensive and fragile, creating a two-tier credit system: cheap capital for mega-cap corporations, expensive and tight capital for mid-market and smaller firms. That redistributes wealth toward large capital and away from entrepreneurship and regional business growth.
